title: DHS Revives Plan to End Work Permits for Spouses of H-1B Workers
excerpt: The regulatory agenda entry signals renewed intent to roll back the 2015 H-4 EAD rule, but the multi-step rulemaking process means no immediate changes for current holders.
body:
• DHS has added a proposal to its 2026 regulatory agenda to remove H-4 dependent spouses from the classes of noncitizens eligible for employment authorization.
  • No immediate changes are in effect — the proposal is classified as a "Long-Term Action" with no timeline set for a proposed rule.
  • An estimated 100,000 Indian spouses hold H-4 EADs, relying on them while facing employment-based green card backlogs of up to 179 years.
  • Separately, the auto-extension of EADs for renewal applicants ended in October 2025, creating work-gap risks even for timely filers.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has placed a proposal on its 2026 federal regulatory agenda to eliminate employment authorization for certain H-4 dependent spouses of H-1B visa holders, reviving an effort that failed during the first Trump administration and raising alarm among tens of thousands of Indian families in the United States.

The proposal, titled "Removing H-4 Dependent Spouses From the Classes of Noncitizens Eligible for Employment Authorization," would reverse a 2015 Obama-era rule that allowed qualifying H-4 spouses to apply for an Employment Authorization Document, or EAD. It has been classified as a "Long-Term Action," with no date set for a formal proposed rule and no draft text available.

No Immediate Impact on Current Holders

Immigration attorneys stress that the regulatory agenda entry is not a final rule. Before any change can take effect, DHS must publish a formal proposed rule, open a public comment period, review submissions, issue a final rule, and set an effective date — a process that takes months at minimum. Any final rule would also face likely legal challenges.

https://x.com/OwenGregorian/status/2094031904936739045

"Don't worry about this just yet. There is a long road between the current proposal and an actual change in the law."

— Jonathan Wasden, Immigration Attorney

Wasden noted that the first Trump administration announced plans to rescind H-4 EAD eligibility in 2017 but never published a proposed rule, partly due to problems with the required economic impact analysis. He added that any new rule would likely have prospective impact, meaning current EAD holders would not necessarily lose their authorization immediately.

Why It Matters for Indian Families

The H-4 EAD has been a lifeline for Indian families caught in one of the world's longest immigration queues. An analysis by the National Foundation for American Policy estimated that more than one million Indians, including dependents, were waiting in the first three employment-based green card categories as of December 2025. An Indian national whose EB-2 petition was filed in January 2026 could face a potential wait of 179 years for permanent residence.

Nearly 100,000 Indian spouses are estimated to hold H-4 EADs. For many — predominantly highly educated Indian women — the document enables them to build careers, earn independent income, and maintain financial stability while their families remain stuck in the green card backlog for years or decades.

The 2015 rule extended work authorization to spouses whose H-1B partners had an approved I-140 immigrant petition or had received H-1B extensions beyond the standard six-year limit under the American Competitiveness in the 21st Century Act. In July 2024, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a lower court ruling affirming that DHS has the legal authority to grant these EADs — a precedent any rescission attempt would need to navigate.

A Separate Blow: Auto-Extension Eliminated

Compounding the uncertainty, DHS eliminated the automatic extension of employment authorization for renewal applicants filing on or after October 30, 2025. Under the previous system, a timely-filed EAD renewal allowed continued work for up to 540 days past expiration. Now, work authorization ends when the card expires, regardless of whether a renewal is pending at USCIS.

With processing times for H-4 EAD renewals ranging from five to twelve months, many applicants face forced employment gaps even when they file at the earliest allowed date — 180 days before expiration. Immigration attorney Henry Lindpere described the rule as "a fundamental shift in how employment authorizations are handled," noting that Indians waiting in long green card queues, H-4 spouses, and international students are among the most vulnerable. Several affected workers have filed lawsuits challenging the change.

What to Watch

The critical moment will be whether DHS publishes an actual proposed rule in the Federal Register. That would open a formal comment period and provide details on whom the rescission would affect and when it would take effect. Until then, existing H-4 work authorization remains valid, and USCIS will continue processing EAD applications for eligible spouses.

Immigration attorneys advise affected families to stay informed, file renewals at the 180-day mark, and coordinate filings with H-1B extensions where possible — but not to treat the regulatory agenda entry as an immediate loss of work rights.
